In Pablo's classroom in Seville, the class hamster, Bolita, needed someone to feed him every day. Nobody wanted the job because the cage smelled.

Pablo, ten, raised his hand. "I'll do it."

Every morning he came ten minutes early, filled the water bottle, added seeds and changed the sawdust on Fridays. When Jana, who was new and shy, watched him, he asked, "Do you want to help?" He showed her how to hold Bolita gently.

One Monday Bolita wasn't eating. Pablo told the teacher straight away, and she called the vet.

Bolita got better. Jana now feeds him on Tuesdays and Thursdays.

Every evening she brought rotis in a steel box. When the puppies were soaked, she got four other kids to collect cardboard and old sacks, and they made a shelter under the stairs.

She made a chart: who feeds, who cleans, which day. Even the watchman helped.

I don't know why she started. She never said. But the puppies waited for her at six every evening.

passage:
Lars, eleven, and his friend Alejandro missed the school bus in Copenhagen by a minute.

Alejandro panicked. "We'll be late! Let's run!"

Lars took a breath. "Wait. Step one: check the timetable." The next bus was in twelve minutes. "Step two: will we be late?" He counted. "Five minutes late." "Step three: tell someone." He called his mother and asked her to message the school.

"Step four: don't run on ice," he said, pointing at the frozen pavement.

They reached school five minutes late. The teacher just nodded. "Thank you for letting us know."

qa.a: The next bus was in twelve minutes.

qa.q: How did Alejandro feel when they missed the bus?
qa.a: Alejandro felt panicked and wanted to run.

qa.a: He checked the timetable, worked out how late they would be, called his mother, and chose not to run on ice.

qa.q: How might the teacher see Lars's call?
qa.a: The teacher appreciated being informed and wasn't upset about the lateness.

During winter exams, Mridul, ten, couldn't find his geometry box on the morning of the maths paper.

His hands went cold. Then he remembered what Madhav Sir always said: "Stop. List. Check."

Stop. He took a breath.

List: last used in the library, then the bus, then his desk.

Check: not in his desk. He ran to the library. Not there. He asked the office for lost-and-found. There it was, with his name on it.

He reached the exam hall two minutes early. Madhav Sir raised his eyebrows. "Found it?"

"Stop, list, check," Mridul said.

The cousins argued, but then agreed. Mridul set an alarm on Papa's phone.

Last year she did homework at midnight, crying. This year she made a timetable on the fridge: 5 to 6 homework, 6 to 6.30 play, 7 to 8 revision. She sticks to it, mostly.

passage:
Pallavi, sit with your Arohi Dida. You want to copy your friend's project? Let me tell you something.

When I was twelve, during the Durga Puja holidays, we had to make a model of a village. My friend Tuku's elder brother made a beautiful one for her. I was jealous.

She said, "Copy mine, change the colours, no one will know."

I nearly did. But I thought, "Then it won't be mine." So I made my own: crooked huts from matchboxes and a pond from a broken mirror.

I got less marks than Tuku. But the teacher kept mine in the display cupboard, because it was clearly done by a child.

On Independence Day when I was nine, our school lined up in the ground for the flag hoisting. It was drizzling.

When the anthem began, Jasleen, next to me, started giggling at a boy who'd slipped in the mud. I wanted to laugh too.

But I remembered my Dadaji, who had been in the army. He always stood very still for the anthem, even at home when it played on television.

So I stood still, hands at my sides, until the last note. Afterwards, Jasleen said, "You're so serious." I said, "Only for fifty-two seconds."

passage:
In Class 9, I kept losing marks in maths, and I thought I was just bad at it. Seema Ma'am asked me to bring my last three test papers.

She didn't correct them. She said, "Look for a pattern."

I went through them at home. I found it. Nearly every mistake was a sign error, a minus that became a plus, in the last step. Not the hard parts. The easy parts, when I was rushing to finish.

It was strange, thinking about how I think. I'd always believed I didn't understand. Actually, I understood; I just didn't check.

So I made myself a rule: finish five minutes early and check signs only.

The next test, I lost two marks instead of eleven. I'm Abhinav, and I still check signs last.

qa.a: Nearly every mistake was a sign error, a minus that became a plus, in the last step.

qa.q: What did Abhinav do after analysing the mistakes?

passage:

This term I asked students to write a weekly reflection on how they study. Indu's entries changed over the term.

In week 1, she wrote, "I read the chapter three times." In week 5, she wrote, "I realised I read it three times but can't explain it. I'm memorising, not understanding."

Friday night

Science class today: Gurleen asked, "What if the moon disappeared?" and Ma'am said, "Think about it for homework."

So I've been thinking. What if?

1. No tides. So fishermen who go out with the tide... would have to change everything.
2. Nights would be much darker. Would more animals hunt at night? Would we need more streetlights?

I don't know if all of this is right. I'll check tomorrow in the library. But it's fun to play it out.

Anjali

In the village near Mandya, the canal water came every week. Anand, fifteen, sat on the bund with Kavitha, his classmate.

"What if the canal stopped for a month?" Kavitha asked.

Anand thought. "Paddy would dry first. Sugarcane maybe lasts longer."

"Then the dairy. No green fodder."

"So milk goes down, and people sell cows."

"And the school bus? It goes on the canal road. If the road cracks..."

Anand laughed. "We've destroyed the whole village in five minutes."

"But seriously," Kavitha said, "what could we do before it happens?"

Anand picked up a stick and drew in the mud: a small pond, a drip line. "We could store water now."

qa.q: Which crop did Anand think would dry first?
qa.a: Paddy would dry first.

qa.q: How did Anand feel playing out the scenario?
qa.a: Anand felt amused but also thoughtful, then serious about planning ahead.

qa.q: How might the village elders see their ideas?
qa.a: The elders might be interested or surprised, seeing young people planning ahead.

grounding: Two rural teenagers ask a what-if question about the canal stopping and play out its effects on the village.

Keerthana, you asked why I get angry when people waste water. Your Rashmi Paati will tell you.

When I was fourteen, our village well never dried. Then a factory came up nearby and dug deep borewells. At the same time, the forest on the hill was cut for a road.

That summer, our well dried in April. Everyone blamed the rain. But I watched: less forest meant the rain ran off instead of sinking in. The factory pumps drew water from underneath. More people came for factory jobs, so more buckets at the well.

I told my father, "It's not the rain. It's everything together." He didn't believe me at first.

Two years later, the panchayat planted trees and made check dams. It took years, but the well filled again.

So, Keerthana, when you waste water, remember it's all connected.

qa.q: When did the well dry that summer?
qa.a: The well dried in April.

qa.q: How did young Rashmi feel when her father didn't believe her?
qa.a: Young Rashmi probably felt frustrated but sure of what she had noticed.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Rashmi's story?
qa.a: When the panchayat planted trees and made check dams, addressing the connected causes, and the well slowly filled again.

qa.q: How might Rashmi's father have seen the well at first?
qa.a: He probably believed the rain was the only cause, like everyone else.

grounding: A grandmother tells how, at fourteen, she saw deforestation, borewells and population growth interact to dry the village well.

The school inspection was on Monday, and the canteen was a mess. Jasleen, sixteen, and Minakshi from the student council had just the weekend to fix the food waste problem.

On Saturday they watched the canteen at lunch. Half the rice was thrown away. Why?

They found several reasons. The portion was fixed, too big for the younger kids. Lunch break was only fifteen minutes, so many didn't finish. And the bins were right by the door, so dumping was easy.

"If we just tell people not to waste, nothing changes," Minakshi said.

So they proposed three things together: two portion sizes, a five-minute longer lunch for the juniors, and moving the bins further in.

On Monday, the inspector asked about waste. Jasleen showed their diagram. "One change alone won't fix it. They're all linked."

qa.q: How long was the lunch break?
qa.a: Lunch break was only fifteen minutes.

qa.q: How did Jasleen feel showing the diagram to the inspector?
qa.a: Jasleen was probably nervous but confident about their understanding of the problem.

qa.q: Why did Jasleen and Minakshi propose several changes at once?
qa.a: They saw that portion size, lunch time and bin placement all interacted, so one change alone wouldn't fix it.

qa.q: How might the younger students be affected by the changes?
qa.a: They would get smaller portions and more time, so they'd waste less and feel less rushed.

grounding: Under time pressure, two teenagers see how portion size, time and bin placement interact to cause canteen waste.

passage:
At the Friday debate club, Lavanya, sixteen, was sure Ishita's argument about school uniforms was wrong. She stood to reply and said, "That's just silly."

The teacher asked, "Why?"

Lavanya opened her mouth and found she had no reason. She didn't like Ishita. They'd fought last month. She had decided the argument was silly because Ishita made it.

She sat down, cheeks hot.

After the debate, she went to Ishita. "Your point about cost was actually good. I dismissed it because... well. I was being unfair."

Ishita blinked. "Okay. Thanks."

That evening Lavanya wrote in her notebook: "Check: am I disagreeing with the idea, or the person?"

qa.q: What did Lavanya write in her notebook?
qa.a: "Check: am I disagreeing with the idea, or the person?"

qa.q: How did Lavanya feel when she realised she had no reason?
qa.a: Lavanya felt embarrassed, her cheeks hot, realising she was biased against Ishita.

qa.q: What did Lavanya do after recognising her bias?
qa.a: She admitted to Ishita that the point was good and she had been unfair, and wrote a reminder to check herself.

qa.q: How might Ishita see Lavanya's apology?
qa.a: Ishita was surprised but likely appreciated the honesty.

grounding: At a debate club, a teenager recognises that personal dislike was biasing her judgement and admits it.

passage:
Dear Neelam Ma'am,

I'm writing because I owe you an apology, and I think I owe myself an explanation.

Last week in class, I argued very strongly that the new exam pattern was unfair. I was sure. I said everyone agreed. When you asked for evidence, I said, "It just is."

I went home and looked it up. I found that the new pattern actually helps students like me in some ways. I had only read posts from people who were angry, and I'd been angry too, so it felt true.

I think I mistook my feeling for a fact. And I only looked at the side I already agreed with.

I'm sorry I was rude. Next time I'll read both sides before I argue.

Sunaina, Class 11 B

qa.q: What did Sunaina say when asked for evidence?
qa.a: Sunaina said, "It just is."

qa.q: How does Sunaina feel writing the letter?
qa.a: Sunaina feels sorry and a bit embarrassed, but also honest and reflective about the mistake.

qa.q: What did Sunaina learn about the limits of personal thinking?
qa.a: That feeling angry made the view seem true, and reading only one side hid the full picture.

qa.q: How might Neelam Ma'am feel reading the letter?
qa.a: Neelam Ma'am would likely feel touched and impressed by the honesty and self-reflection.

grounding: A teenager writes to a teacher recognising emotional reasoning and one-sided reading in an earlier argument.

passage:
Thanks, Sahil. So, I'm Irfan, I'm seventeen, and you asked about the video.

Last year a clip went round of a politician from a party I don't like saying something terrible. I believed it instantly. I shared it with a caption, "Told you so."

My cousin replied, "Check the date." I was annoyed. Obviously it was real, it matched everything I already thought.

Then I checked. It was cut. The full speech said the opposite. The clip had been edited to change the meaning.

I felt so stupid. Not because I was fooled; everyone gets fooled. But because I believed it only because I wanted to.

Now, when something makes me go "Yes! I knew it!", that's exactly when I slow down and check.

qa.q: What did Irfan's cousin reply?
qa.a: The cousin replied, "Check the date."

qa.q: How did Irfan feel after finding out the clip was edited?
qa.a: Irfan felt foolish and embarrassed, realising the belief came from wanting it to be true.

qa.q: What did Irfan change after this experience?
qa.a: Irfan now slows down and checks exactly when something confirms an existing belief.

qa.q: How might Irfan's cousin feel about Irfan's change?
qa.a: The cousin would likely feel glad that the reminder helped.

grounding: A teenager tells a podcast host how confirmation bias led to sharing an edited clip, and how checking comes first now.
